headline: Smithfield Agreement to End Hog Waste Pollution Expires, Leaving North Carolina’s Environmental Crisis Unresolved
deck: A 25-year pact to replace toxic hog waste systems in North Carolina is ending, raising questions about whether the state’s rural communities will ever escape decades of pollution.
body: A quarter-century campaign to end North Carolina’s reliance on toxic hog waste systems is winding down, leaving the state’s most vulnerable residents to face an unresolved environmental crisis. Negotiated in 2000 after Hurricane Fran devastated eastern North Carolina with tens of millions of gallons of spilled hog waste, the Smithfield Agreement was supposed to permanently replace the state’s primitive lagoon and sprayfield system. Instead, the agreement is now concluding without fulfilling its core promise, raising concerns that the pollution and health risks faced by predominantly Black and low-income communities will persist. As the agreement fades, the legacy of industrial hog farming’s environmental damage remains firmly in place.

The disaster that forged the Smithfield Agreement began in September 1996, when Hurricane Fran tore through eastern North Carolina, breaching scores of lagoons that stored untreated hog waste. The storm released millions of gallons of feces and urine into nearby waterways, contaminating drinking supplies and poisoning farmland for miles. The crisis laid bare the dangers of an industry that had long operated with near-impunity, dumping waste into open pits that leaked ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and pathogens into the air and water. For communities living adjacent to these operations, the stench and pollution became an inescapable part of daily life.

In response, then-Attorney General Mike Easley struck a landmark deal with Smithfield Foods, the world’s largest pork producer, to phase out the lagoon system in favor of ‘environmentally superior technologies’ (ESTs). The agreement committed Smithfield to paying up to $2 million annually for 25 years into environmental grants and an additional $15 million for research into alternatives. Easley framed the pact as a historic breakthrough, declaring in a July 2000 press release, ‘I am here today to tell you that we have found a solution that will take us one giant step forward.’
Industry leaders have agreed to fund the development of new technology to replace current lagoon systems. More importantly, they have agreed to implement this technology on their farms immediately.

Yet as the agreement’s final payments near completion, little has changed on the ground. The lagoon and sprayfield system, now decades old, continues to operate across thousands of concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) in the state. Environmental advocates and affected residents argue that the Smithfield Agreement failed to deliver on its central goal: eliminating the pollution that has plagued their communities for generations. The funds and research commitments, while significant, did not translate into widespread adoption of safer waste management practices.

The environmental and health toll of this system has been well-documented. Studies have linked proximity to hog CAFOs with higher rates of respiratory illnesses, infections, and even infant mortality, disproportionately affecting Black and low-income populations. Residents report chronic nosebleeds, headaches, and respiratory distress from the noxious fumes, while water contamination has forced some to rely on bottled supplies. These communities, many of which sit adjacent to sprawling hog farms, have long demanded accountability—demands that went largely unanswered until the Smithfield Agreement offered a glimmer of hope.

Environmental groups now warn that the agreement’s expiration could leave these communities in limbo, with no clear path forward to enforce cleaner waste management. The $15 million in research funding produced prototypes and pilot programs, but the full-scale deployment of ESTs never materialized as promised. Without the binding pressure of the agreement, advocates fear the industry will revert to its old practices, leaving residents to bear the burden of pollution once again.

Smithfield Foods, for its part, has defended its role in the agreement, pointing to the millions invested in research and grants. Yet critics argue that the company’s financial contributions amounted to little more than a PR maneuver, allowing it to avoid stricter regulations while delaying meaningful change. The expiration of the agreement now shifts the burden to state regulators to either enforce new standards or confront the industry’s entrenched resistance.

For the thousands still living in the shadow of these hog operations, the end of the Smithfield Agreement is more than a bureaucratic milestone—it is a reminder of promises broken and justice deferred. The environmental disasters of the 1990s exposed the fragility of North Carolina’s waste management system, but the solutions remain elusive. As the state moves forward, the question lingers: will the next chapter bring real reform, or will the lagoons continue to define the landscape and lives of those who call it home?
The Smithfield Agreement’s failure to deliver on its core promise underscores a harsh truth: environmental justice in North Carolina’s hog country remains a distant goal.
